title: Lesson 16 - Scope, Risk, and Sign-off: Controlling a Salesforce Delivery
description: Leverage the project management lifecycle to deliver a successful solution on time and within scope.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for a new approval step in week nine of a fixed-price build. What is the correct first response?
options: Build it, since goodwill matters more than margin
Refuse, because the scope is locked
Raise a change request with an impact assessment on cost, schedule, and quality
Absorb it into contingency without telling the sponsor
questions.explanation: Every change, whether creep or genuine gain, goes through the same door so the sponsor decides against the triple constraint; absorbing it quietly overspends contingency, and refusing outright removes the client's ability to buy the change.

questions.question: Which single artifact holds risks that have not happened yet, issues that already have, the assumptions your plan rests on, and the dependencies the client owes you?
questions.explanation: Risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies live together in the RAID log so nothing hides in an email thread, and each entry carries an owner and a date; the other artifacts track a single concern apiece.

questions.question: Two weeks before go-live the testers have forty defects open, twelve of them severity 1. Which action protects both the launch date and the client relationship?
options: Go live anyway and fix everything in hypercare
Run a defect triage with the business to agree which severity 1 and 2 items block go-live, then take a scope or date decision to the steering committee
Push go-live and cut scope immediately without a decision meeting
Extend testing indefinitely and stop reporting status
questions.explanation: Triage converts an emotional defect count into an agreed blocking set, and the steering committee is the tier that owns scope and date trade-offs; going live unilaterally and extending without reporting both remove the sponsor's ability to decide.
